extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners (and patent practitioners/responding applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent claims for compliance with the definiteness requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph — i.e., determining whether claim language distinctly and with reasonable particularity delineates the metes and bounds of the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold requirements of clarity and precision
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner’s focus during examination of claims for compliance with the requirement for definiteness of 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, is whether the claim meets the threshold requirements of clarity and precision, not whether more suitable language or modes of expression are available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When satisfied that patentable subject matter is disclosed and claims are directed to such subject matter, examiner should allow claims that define the patentable subject matter with a reasonable degree of particularity and distinctness. Some latitude in manner of expression and aptness of terms should be permitted. Examiners encouraged to suggest improved claim language but should not reject claims merely because they prefer other phrasing if applicant’s language satisfies the statutory requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential inquiry — claims must circumscribe subject matter with reasonable particularity
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential inquiry is whether the claims set out and circumscribe a particular subject matter with a reasonable degree of clarity and particularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definiteness must be analyzed in light of the application disclosure, the teachings of the prior art, and the claim interpretation that would be given by one possessing ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made. Claims must apprise one of ordinary skill in the art of their scope and serve the public notice function (what constitutes infringement). Consider the totality of limitations and their interactions when ascertaining scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claim as a whole in light of disclosure and prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: In reviewing a claim for compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, the examiner must consider the claim as a whole to determine whether the claim apprises one of ordinary skill in the art of its scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the claim in light of (A) the content of the particular application disclosure, (B) the teachings of the prior art, and (C) the claim interpretation a POSITA would give at the time of invention. Use case law (e.g., Solomon v. Kimberly-Clark; In re Larsen) to support totality analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning discernible even if term not used/defined in specification
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim term that is not used or defined in the specification is not indefinite if the meaning of the claim term is discernible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bancorp — components of a compound phrase had well recognized meanings allowing POSITA to infer the entire phrase. If meaning is discernible to POSITA, 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph is satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: When indefiniteness rejection is appropriate (inability to ascertain metes and bounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person of ordinary skill in the art could not interpret the metes and bounds of the claim so as to understand how to avoid infringement, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Morton Int’l. However, if applicant’s language satisfies statutory requirements but examiner merely prefers clearer language, suggest improvements rather than reject. Use 37 CFR 1.105 requirement for additional information if necessary (see MPEP § 704.10).

rubrics_metrics.name: No per se rules — context matters (e.g., use of 'such as')
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere use of the phrase 'such as' in the claim does not by itself render the claim indefinite; Office policy is not to employ per se rules to make technical rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of language held indefinite are fact-specific and listed in MPEP § 2173.05(d). Test for definiteness is whether those skilled in the art would understand what is claimed when read in light of the specification (Orthokinetics). If examiner thinks clarity can be improved (e.g., deletion of 'such as'), they may suggest it but should not pursue a rejection solely on that basis if statutory requirement is met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must establish a clear record when asserting indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: When a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph, is appropriate, the examiner should clearly communicate findings and reasons in an Office action to provide a complete and accurate prosecution record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mere conclusory statements. Provide specific rationales (functional limitations, terms of degree, lack of antecedent basis, etc.). Reference MPEP §§1302.14(I), 707.07(f), 706.03. Clear explanations enhance clarity of prosecution history and help remove uncertainties of claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action must provide sufficient explanation to permit meaningful response
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office action must set forth the specific term or phrase that is indefinite and why the metes and bounds are unclear so the applicant can meaningfully respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain in detail why a term renders claim scope unclear, and whenever practicable indicate how indefiniteness may be resolved (point out specific term/phrase, explain reasoning, indicate practicable remedies). Note claims are given their broadest reasonable interpretation during prosecution to facilitate sharpening/clarifying the claims (In re Buszard). If examiner later withdraws rejection after applicant argument, explain why the position changed and refer to applicant remarks to clarify the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide claim interpretation in reasons for allowance when record is unclear
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prosecution record does not make clear the examiner’s reasons for allowing a claim, the examiner may set forth such reasoning in reasons for allowance (37 CFR 1.104(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before allowance, examiner may specify allowable subject matter and provide reasons. This improves quality and reliability of issued patents by making file history reflect why claims were allowed. Particularly important where allowance follows an interview. Ensure reasons for allowance do not place unwarranted interpretations (broad or narrow) upon claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use interviews to resolve indefiniteness before resorting to rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: When indefiniteness is the only issue, attempt resolution through an interview with the applicant before making a rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews can clarify broadest reasonable interpretation, meaning of claim limitations, scope and clarity of preamble/functional/means-plus-function limitations, etc. Substance of interviews must be made of record in the application. Examples of issues to make of record: why term is/is not sufficiently clear, whether it is inconsistent with the specification, whether it invokes 112, sixth paragraph, and any claim amendments discussed that would resolve ambiguities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth is not indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Breadth of a claim is not to be equated with indefiniteness; a broad claim is not necessarily indefinite if it sufficiently notifies the public of scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Miller and Ultimax: even a formula with many combinations can be definite if it notifies public of scope. Undue breadth should be addressed under other statutory provisions depending on reason: statements outside the application -> 112, second paragraph; lack of support/enabling disclosure -> 112, first paragraph; reads on prior art -> 102/103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence between specification and claims (support/antecedent basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should ideally serve as a glossary to the claim terms so the examiner and public can clearly ascertain meaning; correspondence between the specification and claims is required by 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exact claim terms are not required in the specification if equivalent terms provide needed guidance so meaning is discernable to POSITA (Bancorp). Glossaries are encouraged. If spec lacks needed support or antecedent basis, object under 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) and require applicant to amend description or claims (without introducing new matter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of every term should be apparent (new terminology guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of every term used in a claim should be apparent from the prior art or from the specification and drawings at the time the application is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may use new terms (often desirable for new tech), and new terms are not indefinite just because they don't appear in prior art (In re Fisher). The broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification should be applied. If proposed language is not as precise as subject matter permits, examiner should provide reasons to support indefiniteness and suggest alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms used contrary to ordinary meaning must be redefined in the written description
rubrics_metrics.description: If a term is used contrary to its ordinary meaning, the written description must clearly redefine the term so that POSITA is on notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may act as own lexicographer, but the written description must clearly redefine a claim term to put a reasonable competitor or POSITA on notice (Process Control Corp. v. HydReclaim; Hormone Research Foundation v. Genentech). When more than one definition exists, applicant must make clear which is relied upon; until meaning is clear, 112, second paragraph rejection is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative terminology / terms of degree — provide measurement standard
rubrics_metrics.description: When a term of degree is used in a claim, the examiner should determine whether the specification provides some standard for measuring that degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the spec does not provide a standard, determine whether POSITA could nevertheless ascertain scope (recognized standard in art, examples, figures). Applicant may overcome indefiniteness by submitting a 37 CFR 1.132 declaration showing examples that meet/do not meet the limitation (Enzo Biochem example). If scope remains unclear when read in light of the specification, rejection is proper. Relative terms used where improvement rests on size/weight require greater criticality in disclosure of a standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to a variable object may render a claim indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be rendered indefinite by reference to an object that is variable (e.g., sizing relative to a rider of unspecified build).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with examples where 'so dimensioned as to be insertable through the space between the doorframe of an automobile and one of the seats' was definite because phrase was as accurate as the subject matter permits. Determine whether the reference provides an ascertainable standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance on commonly problematic words/phrases ('about','essentially','substantially','type', other)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific guidance for commonly used ambiguous words: their definiteness depends on context and whether the specification/prior art provide standards or examples to measure the intended scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: • 'About': determine range in context; where specification/prior art provide indication infringement can be assessed (e.g., measurable), term may be definite (Ortho-McNeil; W.L. Gore). • 'Essentially': may be definite if spec contains guidelines/examples to distinguish unavoidable impurities from essential ingredients (In re Marosi). • 'Similar': may be indefinite if unclear what is intended (Ex parte Kristensen/Pappas). • 'Substantially': broad but definite if specification provides general guidelines/examples (In re Nehrenberg; In re Mattison; Andrew Corp. v. Gabriel Electronics). • 'Type': adding 'type' can extend scope and render indefinite if unclear what 'type' conveys (Ex parte Copenhaver; Ex parte Attig). • Other vague phrases ('relatively shallow','of the order of','substantial portion','or like material','comparable','superior') have been held indefinite when spec lacks standard for measuring degree; evaluate against precedent (Ex parte Oetiker; Ex parte Caldwell).
